name: Shackleton rim
note: Point of maximum average illumination on the Shackleton rim (site S in Gläser et al. 2018, 'SR2' in Gläser et al. 2014).
sourceLabel: Gläser et al. 2018, Planet. Space Sci. (NASA NTRS)
description: The rim of Shackleton, a 21 km wide crater almost exactly at the south pole. Spots on the rim see the Sun most of the year, while the crater floor, 4 km lower, has not seen direct sunlight for billions of years and may hold water ice. That contrast is why it is the classic “peak of eternal light” candidate.

photo.caption: Shackleton crater with its permanently dark interior, rendered from Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter data.

name: Connecting Ridge
note: Site C1 on the ridge between Shackleton and de Gerlache; Artemis III candidate region.
sourceLabel: Gläser et al. 2018, Planet. Space Sci. (NASA NTRS)
description: A ridge that links Shackleton and de Gerlache craters. Over a 20-year study it is one of the best-lit places near the pole (about 88% of the time) and it is an Artemis III candidate landing region.

photo.caption: Artemis III candidate regions Connecting Ridge, Connecting Ridge Extension and de Gerlache Rim 1.

name: de Gerlache rim
note: Point C of Bussey et al. 2010; Artemis III candidate region.
sourceLabel: Bryant 2009, JPL IPN Progress Report 42-176; Bussey et al. 2010
description: The rim of de Gerlache, a 32 km crater next to Shackleton. It is lit roughly half of the time and sits right beside permanently shadowed ground; two Artemis III candidate regions lie on this rim.

photo.caption: de Gerlache Rim 1 (upper left) with Connecting Ridge and its extension, Artemis III candidate regions.

name: Nobile rim
note: Point on the NE rim of Nobile crater (Artemis III region 'Nobile Rim 1'); region-level coordinate snapped to the local crest in the LOLA DEM.
sourceLabel: IAU Gazetteer (Nobile) + NASA Artemis III regions 2022
description: The rim of Nobile, a 73 km crater about 165 km from the pole. Artemis III regions “Nobile Rim 1” and “Nobile Rim 2” lie here. Being further from the pole, the Sun climbs a little higher, but surrounding hills block parts of the sky.

photo.caption: Artemis III candidate regions Nobile Rim 1 and Leibnitz Beta Plateau.

name: Malapert massif
note: Point M1 near the Malapert summit. Snapped to the local crest (≤2 km) in the LOLA DEM: the published coordinate comes from a different topography product.
description: A 5 km high mountain about 120 km from the pole. Its upper slopes face Earth almost all the time, which makes it one of the best places near the pole for direct radio contact with home.

photo.caption: Artemis III candidate regions Malapert Massif (upper right) and Haworth.

name: Leibnitz beta plateau
note: Plateau point from Kaguya-based illumination study; now part of 'Mons Mouton Plateau'. Snapped to the local crest (≤2 km) in the LOLA DEM: the published coordinate comes from a different topography product.
description: A high, fairly flat plateau near Mons Mouton, now part of the “Mons Mouton Plateau” Artemis region. Flat high ground is attractive for landing: fewer slopes and long sunlit periods.

photo.caption: Artemis III candidate regions Leibnitz Beta Plateau (left) and Nobile Rim 1.

name: Haworth
note: High ground on the north rim of Haworth crater (Artemis III candidate region); region-level coordinate snapped to the local crest in the LOLA DEM.
sourceLabel: NASA SVS: Artemis III Landing Region Candidates
description: Haworth is a 51 km crater whose floor is permanently shadowed; the candidate region is on its rim. In this app’s terrain model the Malapert massif hides Earth from this spot, so direct communication is poor.

photo.caption: Artemis III candidate regions Haworth (lower left) and Malapert Massif.

name: Mons Mouton
note: Centre of the LROC Mons Mouton Plateau region of interest (former VIPER target, IM-2 area). Snapped to the local crest (≤2 km) in the LOLA DEM: the published coordinate comes from a different topography product.
description: A 6 km tall, flat-topped mountain named after NASA mathematician Melba Roy Mouton. It was the planned target of the VIPER rover, and Intuitive Machines’ IM-2 Athena lander touched down nearby in March 2025.

photo.caption: Mons Mouton with Earth above the horizon, as seen from the lunar south pole.

name: Shackleton floor (PSR)
note: Crater floor, a permanently shadowed region: contrast case for the sunlit rim 10 km away.
description: The floor of Shackleton crater: a permanently shadowed region that has not seen direct sunlight for billions of years. It is one of the coldest places in the Solar System and a prime target in the search for water ice.

photo.caption: Inside the permanently shadowed Shackleton crater, imaged by ShadowCam using light reflected off the sunlit rim (about 2 km across).

name: IM-1 Odysseus
description: Intuitive Machines’ Odysseus landed here on 22 February 2024, the first US landing on the Moon since Apollo 17. It came down about 1.5 km from its target near Malapert A crater on a ~12° slope and tipped onto its side, but kept working for several days.

photo.caption: Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter image of the landing area; the arrow marks the Odysseus lander.

name: Chandrayaan-3 Vikram
note: Landed 2023-08-23 ('Statio Shiv Shakti'). Outside the polar DEM: flat horizon.

name: Apollo 11
note: Tranquility Base, landed 1969-07-20 20:17 UTC. Flat horizon (equatorial contrast case).

name: Apollo 17
note: Taurus-Littrow, landed 1972-12-11. Flat horizon (no polar DEM).
